title: Energetics
learningObjective: know that chemical reactions in which heat energy is given out are described as exothermic, and those in which heat energy is taken in are described as endothermic; describe simple calorimetry experiments for reactions such as combustion, displacement, dissolving and neutralisation; calculate the heat energy change from a measured temperature change using the expression Q = m c Δ T; calculate the molar enthalpy change (ΔH) from the heat energy change, Q; draw and explain energy level diagrams to represent exothermic and endothermic reactions; know that bond-breaking is an endothermic process and that bond-making is an exothermic process; use bond energies to calculate the enthalpy change during a chemical reaction; practical: investigate temperature changes accompanying some of the following types of change: • salts dissolving in water • neutralisation reactions • displacement reactions • combustion reactions.

sections.title: Energetics
sections.markdown:
Every chemical reaction involves an energy change. Some reactions pour heat
out into the surroundings; others pull heat in from them. This chapter is
about measuring those changes, calculating them, and explaining them through
the bonds that break and form while reactions happen.

The chapter runs on two tracks. The **core track** (assessed in both Paper 1C
and Paper 2C) covers the exothermic/endothermic split, the calorimetry
experiments that measure heat changes for combustion, displacement, dissolving
and neutralisation, the equation Q = mc∆T, and the calculation of molar
enthalpy changes. The **chemistry-only track** (Paper 2C, sections marked
3.5C/3.6C/3.7C) adds energy level diagrams and bond-energy calculations. The
practical work — investigating temperature changes when salts dissolve,
neutralisations happen, metals displace and fuels burn — is core practical
work, and the examiners ask about its method, its errors and its
improvements as often as they ask for the numbers.

Two words carry the whole chapter. A reaction that gives out heat is
[[exothermic]]; a reaction that takes heat in is [[endothermic]]. Everything
else — the diagrams, the equations, the experiments — exists to measure,
compare and explain those two directions of energy flow.

:::prior-knowledge
You have already met energy changes without naming them: burning fuels
(Unit 1, states of matter and fuels), metals reacting with acids and the
displacement reactions of the reactivity series (u2:c14), neutralisation
(u2:c16), and the thermal decomposition of carbonates (u2:c10's electrolysis
neighbour, u1:c08's reactions). The mole and molar calculations from
u1:c05/u1:c06 are used in every worked example here — if mol/dm³
concentration sums feel shaky, revise them first.
:::

:::cross-curricular
Physics shares the specific heat capacity idea — the same J/g/°C quantity
appears in thermal physics. Design technology meets it in hand warmers and
self-heating meal packs. Geography uses heat of combustion when comparing
fuels and carbon footprints.
:::

:::exam-hint
In the exam, the command words for this chapter are *know*, *describe*,
*calculate*, *draw* and *explain*. "Know" questions want the exothermic or
endothermic definition in one precise sentence — direction of heat flow
relative to the surroundings. "Describe" questions want a method in logical
order. "Calculate" questions want Q = mc∆T and ΔH = Q ÷ n set out with units.
"Draw" questions (Paper 2C) want labelled energy level diagrams. "Explain"
questions want bonds broken (energy in) versus bonds made (energy out).
:::

:::misconception
"Energy changes only matter for dramatic reactions like explosions." Every
reaction carries an energy change — dissolving a pinch of ammonium chloride
in water lowers the temperature measurably, and neutralising dilute acid with
dilute alkali warms the mixture by several degrees even though nothing
appears to happen. The size differs; the direction of energy flow is always
there.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.1–3.8 energetics items. Before going further, say
in one sentence each: which direction does heat flow in an exothermic
reaction, and what happens to the temperature of the surroundings? Then list
the four reaction families you will measure calorimetrically this chapter.
:::

sections.title: Exothermic reactions
sections.markdown:
A reaction that **gives out heat energy to the surroundings** is called an
[[exothermic]] reaction. Hold a test-tube in which an exothermic reaction is
happening and the tube gets warmer: heat is flowing out of the reaction
mixture into the glass, your fingers and the air. That is the definition and
the observation in one — heat leaves the reaction for the surroundings, and
the temperature of everything around the mixture goes **up**.

The clearest way to see what is happening energetically is to compare the
chemical energy stored in the bonds of the chemicals before and after. In an
exothermic reaction the **products have less chemical energy than the
reactants**. The difference does not vanish — it is converted to heat energy
and released to the surroundings. Chemical energy stored in bonds becomes
heat energy in the environment, so the reaction mixture and its surroundings
warm up.

The classic demonstration is adding water to solid calcium oxide. The heat
produced is enough to boil the water and raise steam, and calcium hydroxide
forms:

CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(s)

The reaction releases so much heat that the water can be seen steaming as the
solid crumbles — a dramatic confirmation that chemical energy has been
converted to heat on a large scale.

:::did-you-know
Calcium oxide is known as [[quicklime]]. Adding water to it is described as
slaking it, and the calcium hydroxide produced is known as slaked lime. The
same chemistry underlies traditional lime mortars, which harden as the
quicklime slakes and then slowly absorbs carbon dioxide from the air.
:::

:::safety
It is less hazardous to use a lump of calcium oxide rather than powdered
calcium oxide, and skin contact must be avoided — the solid is caustic and
the slaking reaction scalds. Wear eye protection.
:::

:::exam-hint
A one-mark "know" question wants exactly this chain: exothermic → heat given
out **to the surroundings** → temperature of the surroundings rises. If the
question then asks you to explain in terms of energy, add the second chain:
products have less chemical energy than reactants → the difference is
released as heat. Saying "it gets hot" without naming the surroundings earns
nothing; the heat flow direction is the mark.
:::

:::misconception
"An exothermic reaction must produce a flame." Flames belong to the small
subset of exothermic reactions that burn — adding water to quicklime, or
dilute acid neutralising dilute alkali, is fiercely exothermic with no flame
at all. The test is the temperature of the surroundings, not light.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.1 exothermic-definition items. Write the definition
of an exothermic reaction without looking, then explain the calcium oxide +
water reaction in terms of the chemical energy of products versus reactants.
Finally, name the product and its common name.
:::

sections.title: Exothermic reactions in action
sections.markdown:
You have already met dozens of [[exothermic]] reactions — this
section gathers the families the examiners expect you to recognise on sight.

**Any reaction that produces a flame is exothermic.** Burning things releases
heat energy. The clearest example is hydrogen burning in oxygen, producing
water and a large amount of heat:

2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)

The burning of hydrogen is used in oxy-hydrogen cutting equipment
underwater, because the flame is hot enough to cut metal even beneath the
surface. You met the same reaction as the test for hydrogen (the squeaky
pop) and in the reactivity-series work.

**Metals reacting with acids** are exothermic. When magnesium reacts with
dilute sulfuric acid, the mixture gets very warm:

Mg(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + H₂(g)

**Neutralisation reactions** are exothermic. About the only interesting thing
you can observe when sodium hydroxide solution reacts with dilute
hydrochloric acid is that the temperature rises:

NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)

Nothing changes colour, no gas bubbles out — but the mixture is measurably
warmer than the two starting solutions. You will measure exactly how much
heat this family releases later in the chapter.

**[[displacement-reaction]]s** are exothermic. The most spectacular example is
the thermite reaction between powdered aluminium and iron(III) oxide, a
displacement (competition) reaction that releases so much heat that the iron
formed is molten — the reaction is used to weld railway lines together:

2Al(s) + Fe₂O₃(s) → 2Fe(l) + Al₂O₃(s)

:::exam-hint
"Give two examples of exothermic reactions" is a gift question if you keep a
mental list: combustion (hydrogen, or any fuel), metal + acid,
neutralisation, displacement. Name the chemicals, not just the family —
"magnesium with dilute sulfuric acid" scores; "a reaction that gets hot" does
not. If asked for equations, any balanced equation from this section is safe.
:::

:::misconception
"Neutralisation cannot be exothermic because salt solution does not feel
warm." With dilute solutions the temperature rise is only a few degrees —
real, measurable with a thermometer, but easy to miss with a finger. The
thermometer, not your hand, decides whether a reaction is exothermic; later
in this chapter the measured rise for KOH + HCl works out at ΔH = −55.4
kJ/mol.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.1 exothermic-examples items. List the four
exothermic families from memory, write a balanced equation for one member of
each family, and state what you would observe (other than a flame) for the
metal + acid and neutralisation examples.
:::

sections.title: Enthalpy change (∆H)
sections.markdown:
You can measure the amount of heat energy taken in or released in a chemical
reaction. It is called the [[enthalpy-change]] of the reaction and is given
the symbol ∆H. ∆H is pronounced "delta H" — the Greek letter ∆ is used to
mean "change in", so ∆H means "change in heat". One subtlety matters: it is
not possible to measure how much enthalpy (H) a substance *has* — you can
only measure the **change** in enthalpy when it reacts. The enthalpy change
is the amount of heat energy taken in or given out in a chemical reaction;
it is the difference between the energy of the products and the energy of
the reactants.

∆H is given a minus or a plus sign to show whether heat is being given out
or absorbed, and you always read the sign from the point of view of the
reactants. For an exothermic reaction, ∆H is **negative**, because the
reactants are losing energy as heat — heat is transferred to the
surroundings, which then get warmer. ∆H is measured in units of kJ/mol
(kilojoules per mole); you may also see the units written kJ mol⁻¹.

Written next to an equation, the enthalpy change looks like this:

Mg(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + H₂(g)   ∆H = −466.9 kJ/mol

The ∆H here represents the enthalpy change of the reaction: 466.9 kJ of heat
is given out when one mole of magnesium reacts in this way. You know heat
has been given out because ∆H carries a negative sign.

The word [[stability]] describes the relative energies of reactants and
products: **the more energy a chemical has, the less stable it is.** So when
an exothermic reaction runs, the products (lower energy) are more stable than
the reactants — energy has drained out of the chemicals into the
surroundings. And remember the vocabulary: the reactants are the chemicals
you start with. The per-mole basis is why the [[mole]] matters here — every
∆H you quote is for the amounts shown in the balanced equation.

:::key-point
∆H is the enthalpy change: the heat energy taken in or given out by a
reaction, measured from the reactants' point of view. Negative ∆H = heat
given out (exothermic). Positive ∆H = heat taken in (endothermic). Units:
kJ/mol (equivalently kJ mol⁻¹).
:::

:::exam-hint
Two habits earn the sign-and-units marks every time. First, never quote a
∆H without its sign — an answer of "466.9 kJ/mol" for the magnesium reaction
above loses the mark that "−466.9 kJ/mol" scores. Second, keep the units per
mole: if a question gives you heat in joules for 0.78 g of fuel, dividing by
moles before quoting kJ/mol is part of the calculation, not decoration (the
full method arrives in the worked example later in this chapter).
:::

:::misconception
"A negative ∆H means energy is missing." The minus sign records a **loss
from the reactants**, not a loss from the universe: the heat has been
transferred to the surroundings, where it warms them up. Energy is
conserved — the sign just says which way it flowed relative to the chemicals.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.4 enthalpy-change items. Define enthalpy change,
state why exothermic reactions carry a negative ∆H, and write the two
acceptable forms of the units. Then explain why a chemical with more energy
is described as less stable.
:::

sections.title: Showing an exothermic change on an energy level diagram
sections.markdown:
An [[energy-level-diagram]] is the standard picture for the energy story of a
reaction. The vertical axis is energy (label it!), the horizontal axis is
the progress of the reaction, and the reactants and products each sit on
their own horizontal level.

For an **exothermic** reaction the reactants sit **higher** than the
products — they have more chemical energy — so the arrow from reactants to
products points **down**. The drop between the two levels is the energy that
has been released to the surroundings as heat. Because the products have less
energy, we say the products are **more stable** than the reactants. As the
reaction runs, the temperature of both the reaction mixture and its
surroundings goes up — that warming is the released energy showing itself.

Draw the diagram in this order and you cannot lose the labels:

1. Two horizontal levels — reactants on the upper level, products on the
   lower level.
2. Vertical axis labelled "energy", horizontal axis labelled "progress of
   the reaction".
3. An arrow pointing down from reactants to products.
4. ∆H written next to the arrow with its **negative** sign — the drop is the
   magnitude, the sign records the direction.

:::exam-hint
Paper 2C loves three details on this diagram. Label both axes — an unlabelled
energy axis costs the mark even if the shape is perfect. Put the reactants
above the products for an exothermic change, with a downward arrow. And
write ∆H beside the arrow **with its minus sign**; "∆H" alone, or a positive
value on a downward diagram, contradicts itself and loses the mark. If the
question asks you to *explain* the shape, one sentence does it: the products
have less chemical energy than the reactants, so the difference is released
as heat.
:::

:::misconception
"The products are drawn lower because the reaction mixture ended up colder."
The levels show **chemical energy stored in the chemicals**, not the
temperature at the end. An exothermic reaction leaves the *surroundings*
hotter precisely because the *chemicals* ended with less energy — the two
observations point in opposite directions, and the diagram records the
chemicals.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.5C energy-level-diagram items. Sketch the
exothermic energy level diagram from memory: axes, levels, arrow, sign.
Then answer cold — for the reaction Mg + H₂SO₄ (ΔH = −466.9 kJ/mol), which
level is higher and what does the drop represent?
:::

sections.title: Endothermic reactions
sections.markdown:
A reaction that **absorbs heat from the surroundings** is called an
[[endothermic]] reaction. Hold a test-tube in which an endothermic reaction
is happening and the tube gets **colder** — heat is flowing the other way,
out of your fingers and the air and into the reaction mixture.

In energy terms the picture mirrors the exothermic case exactly. In an
endothermic reaction the **products have more chemical energy than the
reactants**. To supply the extra energy needed to convert low-energy
reactants into high-energy products, heat energy is absorbed from the
surroundings and converted to chemical energy stored in the new bonds. The
temperature of the reaction mixture and the surroundings goes **down**
because heat energy has been drained and converted into a different form.

Chemical cold packs work on exactly this principle: an endothermic reaction
inside the pack absorbs heat from the surroundings, lowering the temperature
of the injured arm it rests against.

The everyday laboratory example is the [[thermal-decomposition]] of metal
carbonates, which you met with Group 2 chemistry. These are endothermic —
you have to heat a carbonate **constantly** to make it decompose, because
the reaction keeps drawing heat from the flame. Copper(II) carbonate (green)
decomposes on heating to produce copper(II) oxide (black):

CuCO₃(s) → CuO(s) + CO₂(g)

Zinc carbonate decomposes similarly to form zinc oxide when heated.

One warning that examiners turn into questions: **not every reaction that
needs heating is endothermic.** Sometimes we heat a mixture simply to make
the reaction go faster — the burning of magnesium needs a hot flame to start
it, yet the reaction itself is fiercely exothermic. The direction of the
temperature change *during* the reaction tells you which kind you have; the
presence of a Bunsen burner does not.

:::exam-hint
The examiner's favourite endothermic definition question adds a twist:
"explain why the decomposition of copper(II) carbonate is endothermic." The
full-mark chain is: the products have **more** chemical energy than the
reactants → the extra energy must be absorbed from the surroundings as heat
→ so the temperature of the surroundings falls and heating must continue
throughout the reaction. Keep the heating-continuously point — it is what
separates an endothermic decomposition from a merely slow reaction.
:::

:::misconception
"If you have to light a Bunsen burner, the reaction must be endothermic."
Heat applied to *start* or *speed up* a reaction tells you nothing about the
direction of the overall energy change. Magnesium burning needs a flame to
get going and then releases far more heat than it absorbed. Classify by the
temperature change of the mixture itself: drops during the change →
endothermic; rises → exothermic.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.1 endothermic-definition items. Define an
endothermic reaction, state the energy relationship between products and
reactants, write the equation for the thermal decomposition of copper(II)
carbonate, and explain why a reaction needing a flame to start is not
necessarily endothermic.
:::

sections.title: Showing an endothermic change on an energy level diagram
sections.markdown:
The endothermic [[energy-level-diagram]] is the mirror image of the exothermic
one. In an endothermic change the **products have more energy than the
reactants**, so we say the products are **less stable** than the reactants.
That extra energy has to come from somewhere, and it is taken from the
surroundings — for the thermal decomposition of carbonates in the laboratory,
it comes from the Bunsen burner.

Because the reactants are **gaining** energy, the enthalpy change of the
reaction is given a **positive** sign. The thermal decomposition of calcium
carbonate carries the value you should be able to quote and explain:

CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g)   ∆H = +178 kJ/mol

This means that 178 kJ of heat energy must be absorbed to convert one mole
of calcium carbonate into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. On the diagram,
the arrow from reactants to products points **up**, the products level sits
**above** the reactants level, and ∆H is written beside the arrow with its
plus sign. Label the vertical axis "energy" and the horizontal axis "progress
of the reaction" exactly as before.

:::exam-hint
Paper 2C asks for both diagrams in a single question so the comparison marks
are easy to bank: exothermic = products lower, ∆H negative, arrow down;
endothermic = products higher, ∆H positive, arrow up. For the calcium
carbonate example, quote the value *with* its plus sign and attach the
meaning — "178 kJ absorbed **per mole** of calcium carbonate decomposed."
Omitting "per mole" leaves the answer incomplete; the value is defined for
the equation's amounts.
:::

:::misconception
"The +178 kJ/mol is the total heat the Bunsen burner supplied." The value is
the minimum absorbed **by the reaction** per mole of calcium carbonate
decomposed — the burner also heats the tube, the air and everything else,
which is why a real flame delivers far more than 178 kJ in practice. The
quoted ∆H is the reaction's share, not the fuel bill.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.5C endothermic-diagram items. Draw the endothermic
energy level diagram for CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ with every label, then state the
meaning of ∆H = +178 kJ/mol in one sentence. Finally, name where the energy
comes from in the laboratory and what that does to the surroundings.
:::

sections.title: Specific heat capacity and the Q = mc∆T equation
sections.markdown:
When we heat something up, it gets hotter. The [[specific-heat-capacity]]
tells us how much energy has to be put in to increase the temperature of
something. It is defined as **the amount of heat needed to raise the
temperature of 1 gram of a substance by 1 °C**. The unit is J/g/°C (or
J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹).

For water the value is **4.18 J/g/°C** — 4.18 J of heat energy raises the
temperature of 1 g of water by 1 °C. The idea scales in both directions, and
the multiplication is easy to reason through:

- 1 g of water by 2 °C needs 4.18 × 2 = 8.36 J.
- 2 g of water by 2 °C needs 2 × 8.36 = 16.72 J.

The heat energy required is **directly proportional** to the mass (m) and to
the temperature change (∆T), which compresses the whole idea into one
equation — the workhorse of this chapter:

**heat energy change = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change**

**Q = m × c × ∆T**

Each symbol carries a discipline. Q is the heat energy change in joules. m
is the mass **of the substance being heated** (in grams — usually water). c
is that substance's specific heat capacity (4.18 J/g/°C for water). ∆T is
its temperature change in °C. The same equation runs backwards for cooling:
to cool 1 g of water by 1 °C you must remove 4.18 J, so an endothermic
process sitting in water still hands you a usable Q — you just read the
temperature drop.

A [[calorimeter]] is simply the container you run a calorimetry experiment
in: in one experiment it is a copper can, in others a polystyrene cup. What
matters is that the reaction's heat ends up changing the temperature of a
known mass of water inside it.

:::key-point
The unit of specific heat capacity is J/g/°C (J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹). Water's value is
4.18 J/g/°C — memorise it, every calculation in this chapter uses it. The
∆ in ∆T is the same "change in" symbol as in ∆H, this time applied to
temperature, and the equation applies to cooling as well as heating.
:::

:::exam-hint
Q = mc∆T questions are won and lost on *which mass* and *which ∆T* you
substitute. m is the mass of the **water (or solution) being heated**, never
the mass of the solid burned or dissolved. ∆T is final minus initial (or the
magnitude of the drop for cooling processes). Carry an extra significant
figure through the calculator and round at the end; divide by 1000 to
convert J to kJ before computing a ∆H in kJ/mol.
:::

:::misconception
"Specific heat capacity is a property of heating only." The quantity
describes energy needed *per degree of temperature change in either
direction* — removing 4.18 J cools 1 g of water by 1 °C just as supplying
4.18 J warms it. Endothermic experiments in this chapter depend on the
cooling direction: the reaction takes heat from the water, ∆T is a drop, and
Q still comes out of the same equation.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.3 Q=mc∆T items. State the definition and unit of
specific heat capacity, calculate the energy needed to warm 50 g of water
from 20.0 °C to 35.0 °C, and name the container used in a calorimetry
experiment with the two common laboratory examples.
:::

sections.title: Calorimetry and the combustion-of-an-alcohol experiment
sections.markdown:
Measuring the heat absorbed or given out by a reaction is
[[calorimetry]], and it is more straightforward than the name suggests. The
idea: let the reaction's heat change the temperature of a known mass of
water, then use Q = mc∆T to calculate the heat released. The mass, specific
heat capacity and temperature change all belong to **the substance heated**
— the water. If you also know how many moles of reactant were used up, you
can divide Q by n to reach the molar enthalpy change ∆H in kJ/mol.

The classic International GCSE experiment measures the heat given off when
small alcohols burn — methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol. The
alcohol burns in a small spirit burner and the heat produced warms water in
a copper can (the calorimeter). The molar enthalpy change of combustion is
how much heat energy is released when **one mole** of the alcohol burns.

The procedure, in the order that earns method marks:

1. Measure **100 cm³ of cold water** with a measuring cylinder and transfer
   it to the copper can.
2. Take the **initial temperature** of the water.
3. Weigh a spirit burner containing the alcohol **with its lid on** — the
   lid stays on whenever the wick is not lit, to stop the alcohol
   evaporating.
4. Arrange the apparatus so the burner can heat the water in the can, and
   shield it as far as possible to prevent draughts.
5. Light the wick. Stop heating when the water has a reasonable temperature
   rise (about 40.0 °C); extinguish the flame by putting the lid back on the
   wick.
6. Stir the water thoroughly and measure the **maximum temperature**.
7. Weigh the spirit burner again with its lid on.
8. Repeat with the same alcohol to check reliability, then repeat with other
   alcohols.

How big a temperature rise should you aim for? There is no ideal answer — it
is a deliberate compromise. The higher the temperature the water reaches,
the greater the heat losses to the surroundings during the experiment; but
if you only warm the water a little, errors in reading the thermometer and
in finding the small mass change of the alcohol become too significant. A
rise of around 40 °C balances the two.

:::safety
Wear eye protection. Never carry a lit spirit burner, and never fill or
re-fill one when there is a naked flame nearby. Keep the lid on the burner
whenever the wick is not lit.
:::

:::key-point
The enthalpy change when 1 mole of a substance is burned is called the
[[enthalpy-change-of-combustion]]. Every combustion result in this chapter
is quoted per mole of fuel burned.
:::

:::exam-hint
Method questions on this experiment reward the *control* details: lid on
when not lit (stops evaporation changing the mass), shielding from draughts
(cuts heat loss), stir before reading (distributes the heat so the maximum
is true), weigh the burner *with* the lid both times. If asked for an
improvement, "use a lid or shield around the can to reduce heat loss" or
"a wind shield to prevent draughts" are the standard reliable answers.
:::

:::misconception
"The mass to use in Q = mc∆T is the mass of alcohol that burned." The Q
equation describes the **water**: m is the 100 g of water in the can (100
cm³ × density 1 g/cm³). The mass of alcohol burned — the change in the
burner's reading — enters later, when you convert Q into a per-mole value.
Mixing the two masses up is the single most common arithmetic error on this
experiment.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.2 + 3.8 combustion-calorimetry items. List the
procedure in order from memory, then answer: why does the burner lid go back
on between weighings, why shield the flame, and what temperature rise do you
aim for — with the reason it is a compromise?
:::

sections.title: Worked example: the combustion calculation
sections.markdown:
Combustion is exothermic, so the temperature of the water goes up; as the
ethanol burns, the total mass of burner plus ethanol goes down. Here is a
complete data set and the full route from it to a molar enthalpy change of
combustion — the calculation the examiner asks you to reproduce with fresh
numbers.

| Measurement | Value |
|---|---|
| Volume of water / cm³ | 100 |
| Mass of burner + ethanol before / g | 137.36 |
| Mass of burner + ethanol after / g | 136.58 |
| Original temperature of water / °C | 21.5 |
| Final temperature of water / °C | 62.8 |

:::worked-example
**Find the molar enthalpy change of combustion of ethanol from the data
above.**

*Step 1 — temperature change.* ∆T = 62.8 − 21.5 = **41.3 °C**.

*Step 2 — mass of water.* 100 cm³ of water has mass **100 g** (density of
water ≈ 1 g/cm³ at room temperature).

*Step 3 — heat gained by the water.* c = 4.18 J/g/°C (it is the water that
is being heated):

Q = mc∆T = 100 × 4.18 × 41.3 = 17 260 J

Divide by 1000 to convert to kJ: Q = **17.26 kJ**. This is the heat released
by the ethanol burned in this experiment.

*Step 4 — moles of ethanol burned.* Mass burned = 137.36 − 136.58 = **0.78 g**.
Ethanol, C₂H₅OH, has relative molecular mass (2 × 12) + (5 × 1) + 16 + 1 =
**46**:

n = mass ÷ Mr = 0.78 ÷ 46 = **0.01696 mol**

*Step 5 — molar enthalpy change.* The [[molar-enthalpy-change]] is the heat
energy change divided by the number of moles burned:

∆H = Q ÷ n = −17.26 ÷ 0.01696 = −1017.7 ≈ **−1020 kJ/mol** (3 s.f.)

Written on the equation:

CH₃CH₂OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O   ∆H = −1020 kJ/mol

The negative sign shows heat is released — the combustion is exothermic, as
the rising temperature already told you.
:::

:::key-point
The [[enthalpy-change-of-combustion]] is defined for **one mole** of
substance burned — that is why Step 4 exists. Quoting −17.26 kJ as a final
answer confuses the heat released *in the experiment* with the per-mole
quantity the question asked for.
:::

:::exam-hint
Two technique rules decide whether the arithmetic marks survive to the end.
First, significant figures: quote the final answer to 3 significant figures,
carry more figures through the calculator, and round only at the end — the
least precise piece of experimental data fixes how many figures your answer
can honestly carry. Second, the sign: add it at the ∆H stage and sanity-check
it against the temperature change. Temperature went **up** → exothermic →
∆H **negative**. Temperature down → endothermic → ∆H positive. A
sign-and-trend mismatch means a step has gone wrong.
:::

:::misconception
"Rounding at every step keeps the working tidy." Rounding early compounds:
0.01696 mol rounded to 0.02 mol turns −1017.7 kJ/mol into −863 kJ/mol — off
by more than 150 kJ and outside the mark scheme's tolerance. Keep the
calculator's full display until the final line, then round once.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.3 + 3.4 combustion-calculation items. Redo the
five steps with the burner masses 200.00 g and 199.30 g, the same 100 cm³ of
water warming from 20.0 °C to 54.0 °C, and butan-1-ol (Mr = 74). Check: your
Q = 14 212 J, your n = 0.00946 mol, and your answer near −1500 kJ/mol with
a minus sign.
:::

sections.title: Evaluating the combustion experiment
sections.markdown:
How accurate was the −1020 kJ/mol obtained for ethanol? Data booklets quote
an accepted value of **−1370 kJ/mol** for the enthalpy change of combustion
of ethanol — 1370 kJ of heat should be given out when one mole burns. The
experimental value is **less exothermic** than expected: the experiment
seemed to give out less heat than it should have. Explaining that gap is a
guaranteed exam question, and the answer has two parts.

**Heat loss dominates.** The warm water gives out heat to the air; heat from
the flame escapes straight into the surroundings rather than into the water;
and heat is used to raise the temperature of the copper can and the
thermometer as well as the water. Every joule that takes those side-routes
is a joule the Q = mc∆T calculation never sees, so the measured temperature
rise is too small and the calculated ∆H is too little exothermic.

**The combustion is incomplete.** [[incomplete-combustion]] happens when
there is not enough oxygen present, and it releases **less** heat than
complete combustion. You can see the evidence directly: the flame of the
wick is often yellow-orange rather than blue, and soot (carbon) collects on
the bottom of the copper can. In complete combustion the flame is blue and
carbon dioxide is produced instead of carbon. Both observations — flame
colour and soot — are acceptable evidence in the exam.

When the same experiment is repeated across the alcohol family, a pattern
emerges. Plotting the molar enthalpy change of combustion against the number
of carbon atoms in the alcohol shows the combustion reaction getting **more
exothermic as the alcohol chain becomes longer** — longer alcohols give out
more heat energy per mole when they burn than shorter ones. The increase is
**regular**: each step from one alcohol to the next adds one extra CH₂ unit,
so the number of extra bonds broken and made increases in a regular way, and
so does the heat evolved.

One plotting discipline belongs with that graph. The points should be joined
as **discrete points, not a smooth curve**: a smooth curve is only correct
for a continuous independent variable — one that can take any value. There
is no such thing as an alcohol with 0.5 or 1.64 carbon atoms; the number of
carbon atoms is non-continuous, so a line through the points can mislead.
The comparison remains valid: repeat with other alcohols under conditions as
similar as possible, and the trend in heat evolved with chain length is
reliable.

:::key-point
Evaluation formula for this experiment: measured ∆H less exothermic than the
data booklet → (1) heat lost to surroundings (air, can, thermometer), (2)
incomplete combustion (yellow-orange flame, soot) because less heat is
released when oxygen is short.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Suggest why the student's value differs from the data book value" wants the
two-part answer above, with **evidence**. State the heat-loss routes
specifically (to the air, from the flame, into the can and thermometer), then
quote an observation for incomplete combustion — soot on the can or a
yellow-orange flame instead of blue. For the improvement question,
"insulate the can / add a lid / shield from draughts" attacks heat loss;
"burn the alcohol in plenty of oxygen" attacks incompleteness. Match each
improvement to the error it fixes.
:::

:::misconception
"A value of −1020 kJ/mol instead of −1370 kJ/mol means the arithmetic was
wrong." The arithmetic is fine; the *method* is systematically imperfect.
Heat escaping to the surroundings and incomplete combustion both push the
measured temperature rise down, and a smaller ∆T produces a smaller — less
exothermic — ∆H. The gap's direction is predictable, which is exactly what
makes it a favourite evaluation question.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.2 + 3.8 experiment-evaluation items. List the
three heat-loss routes, give two observations that prove the combustion was
incomplete, and state the trend in ∆H of combustion as alcohol chain length
increases — with the reason the increase is regular.
:::

sections.title: Calorimetry for reactions in solution
sections.markdown:
Very similar methods to the alcohol experiment measure molar enthalpy
changes for three more reaction families:

- **displacement reactions** — for example zinc metal in copper(II) sulfate
  solution;
- **dissolving** — for example ammonium chloride dissolving in water to form
  a solution;
- **neutralisation reactions** — for example potassium hydroxide solution
  with dilute hydrochloric acid.

These experiments also involve "heating water" — but this time the water is
part of the solutions themselves. The reaction happens in (or into) a
polystyrene cup, the solution warms or cools, and the same equation Q = mc∆T
converts the temperature change into heat energy. Two assumptions do the
converting, and you must be able to state both:

1. the **density** of the solution is the same as that of water, so 1 cm³ of
   solution has a mass of 1 g;
2. the **specific heat capacity** of the mixture is the same as that of
   water — reasonable, because the reaction mixture is mostly water.

From there the route to the [[molar-enthalpy-change]] is identical to the
combustion example: Q = mc∆T for the heat, moles of the limiting reactant
for n, then ∆H = Q ÷ n with the sign fixed by whether the temperature rose
(exothermic, negative) or fell (endothermic, positive). The next three
sections run the full procedure and calculation for each family in turn.

:::exam-hint
"Describe how to measure the enthalpy change of neutralisation" and its
siblings for displacement and dissolving are describe-the-method questions:
polystyrene cup in a beaker (insulation), measured volumes, initial
temperature, add and stir, record maximum (or minimum) temperature. Then the
assumption pair — density of solution = density of water, and specific heat
capacity of mixture = 4.18 J/g/°C because the mixture is mostly water —
usually sits on the mark scheme as its own line. Learn it verbatim once and
reuse it for all three families.
:::

:::misconception
"Each reaction family needs a different equation." The equation never
changes: Q = mc∆T, then ∆H = Q ÷ n. What changes is *what reacts* (a metal
and a salt solution, a salt and water, an acid and an alkali) and therefore
*which moles* you divide by. The constant structure is why one worked
example per family is enough preparation for all of them.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.2 solution-calorimetry items. Name the three
solution-reaction families, state the two standard assumptions of the
method, and write the two-step calculation route from temperature change to
molar enthalpy change.
:::

sections.title: Practical: measuring the enthalpy change of a displacement reaction
sections.markdown:
To determine the enthalpy change for the [[displacement-reaction]] between zinc
and copper(II) sulfate, the procedure is:

1. Place a polystyrene cup in a 250 cm³ glass beaker.
2. Transfer **50 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ copper(II) sulfate solution** into the
   cup using a measuring cylinder.
3. Weigh **1.20 g of zinc** using a weighing boat on a balance.
4. Record the **initial temperature** of the copper(II) sulfate solution.
5. Add the zinc.
6. Stir the solution as quickly as possible.
7. Record the **maximum temperature** reached.

| Measurement | Value |
|---|---|
| Initial temperature of copper(II) sulfate solution / °C | 17.0 |
| Maximum temperature of the reaction mixture / °C | 27.3 |

The calculation uses the same assumptions as every solution experiment: the
solution's density is that of water (1 cm³ has mass 1 g) and its specific
heat capacity is 4.18 J/g/°C, because the mixture is mostly water.

:::worked-example
**Calculate the enthalpy change for this displacement reaction when 1 mole
of copper(II) sulfate reacts with zinc.**

*Step 1 — heat given out.* ∆T = 27.3 − 17.0 = 10.3 °C:

Q = mc∆T = 50 × 4.18 × 10.3 = 2152.7 J = 2.1527 kJ

*Step 2 — which reactant runs out first?* Moles of CuSO₄ = (50 ÷ 1000) ×
0.200 = **0.0100 mol**. Moles of Zn = 1.20 ÷ 65 = **0.0185 mol**. One mole
of Zn reacts with one mole of CuSO₄, so 0.0100 mol of CuSO₄ reacts with
0.0100 mol of Zn — we added 0.0185 mol of zinc, so the zinc is in
[[excess]] and the **copper(II) sulfate is the limiting reactant**.
(Excess means more than enough is present to ensure all the copper(II)
sulfate reacts.)

*Step 3 — per mole.* The heat released when 1 mole of CuSO₄ reacts is:

∆H = Q ÷ n = 2.1527 ÷ 0.0100 = 215.3 ≈ **−215 kJ/mol**

Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)   ∆H = −215 kJ/mol

The negative sign is added because the temperature of the reaction mixture
went up: the displacement is exothermic and heat is released. (Remember the
÷1000 when converting the 50 cm³ to dm³ — the concentration is given in
mol/dm³.)
:::

You could repeat this experiment with metals of different reactivities: the
more reactive the metal, the more heat should be released in the
displacement. Keep everything else the same — the number of moles of metal,
the size of the solid particles, and the volume and concentration of the
copper(II) sulfate solution. **Do not use metals more reactive than
magnesium**: those react with the water itself, and you would be measuring
the heat released by the metal–water reaction instead.

:::key-point
The moles you divide Q by are the moles of the **limiting reactant** — the
chemical that is not in excess. In this experiment the zinc was deliberately
in excess so that all 0.0100 mol of copper(II) sulfate reacted, making the
per-mole division clean.
:::

:::exam-hint
The examiner builds this question in three layers: the Q = mc∆T arithmetic
(2 marks), the moles comparison that identifies the excess reactant (1–2
marks), and the division plus sign (2 marks). The layer candidates drop is
the middle one — *say explicitly* that 0.0185 mol of zinc exceeds the
0.0100 mol of copper(II) sulfate, so copper(II) sulfate is limiting and its
moles go in the denominator of ∆H = Q ÷ n. A final answer without the
negative sign, or divided by the zinc's moles, loses the last two marks.
:::

:::misconception
"Use the moles of the reactant you weighed, because its mass was measured."
The per-mole definition attaches to the balanced equation's reacting ratio,
not to whichever mass was easier to weigh. With zinc in excess, dividing by
0.0185 mol would understate the per-mole value; the reaction's heat belongs
to the 0.0100 mol of copper(II) sulfate that actually reacted.
:::

:::safety
Wear eye protection and avoid skin contact with the salts and their
solutions.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.2 + 3.4 + 3.8 displacement-calorimetry items.
Run the three-layer calculation with 50 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ CuSO₄ and 1.30
g of zinc (Ar = 65): identify the limiting reactant, show which moles divide
Q, and justify the sign of ∆H. Check: n(CuSO₄) = 0.00500 mol, n(Zn) =
0.0200 mol, zinc in excess.
:::

sections.title: Practical: measuring the enthalpy change when a salt dissolves
sections.markdown:
Calorimetry also measures the heat given out or taken in when salts dissolve
in water. The set-up is the same polystyrene cup in a 250 cm³ beaker used
for the displacement experiment. For ammonium chloride:

1. Place a polystyrene cup in a 250 cm³ glass beaker.
2. Transfer **100 cm³ of water** into the cup using a measuring cylinder.
3. Record the **initial temperature** of the water.
4. Weigh **5.20 g of ammonium chloride** using a weighing boat on a balance.
5. Add the ammonium chloride to the water and stir vigorously until it has
   all dissolved.
6. Record the **minimum temperature**.

| Measurement | Value |
|---|---|
| Initial temperature of water / °C | 18.3 |
| Minimum temperature of salt solution / °C | 15.1 |

The temperature **decreases**, so the process is endothermic — heat is
absorbed from the surroundings for the dissolving to occur. Note one
difference of kind, not just of sign: [[dissolving]] is a **physical
process** rather than a chemical reaction. When some salts dissolve heat is
given out (exothermic); when others dissolve the process is endothermic —
ammonium chloride belongs to the second group.

The calculation follows the standard assumptions: the diluted solution has
the specific heat capacity of water (it is mostly water), and the mass of
the solution is 100 g — the small mass of ammonium chloride is ignored. Heat
absorbed from the surrounding air is a further source of error, one that
matters much more here than in the hotter experiments.

:::worked-example
**Calculate the molar enthalpy change for dissolving ammonium chloride in
water.**

*Step 1 — heat absorbed.*

Q = mc∆T = 100 × 4.18 × (18.3 − 15.1) = 100 × 4.18 × 3.2 = 1337.6 J =
**1.3376 kJ**

*Step 2 — moles dissolved.* The relative formula mass of ammonium chloride,
NH₄Cl, is 14 + (4 × 1) + 35.5 = **53.5**:

n = mass ÷ Mr = 5.20 ÷ 53.5 = **0.0972 mol**

*Step 3 — per mole.* The [[molar-enthalpy-change]] of solution:

∆H = Q ÷ n = 1.3376 ÷ 0.0972 = **+13.8 kJ/mol**

The **positive** sign shows that heat is absorbed — dissolving ammonium
chloride in water is an endothermic process, which is why the temperature
went down.
:::

:::key-point
Dissolving is a physical process. The direction of its temperature change
depends on the salt: some dissolvings warm the water (exothermic), others
cool it (endothermic). Read the thermometer — do not assume.
:::

:::exam-hint
Two marks hide in the details here. The thermometer reads a **minimum** for
this experiment — "maximum temperature" is copy-paste from the exothermic
experiments and drops the observation mark. And the sign discipline inverts:
temperature **down** → endothermic → ∆H **positive**. If asked why the
assumptions are reasonable, the answer is that the solution is mostly water,
so it inherits water's specific heat capacity; if asked for a major error,
heat absorbed from the surrounding air during the (slow) dissolving is the
honest one.
:::

:::misconception
"Endothermic means the thermometer reads a lower number because the
thermometer is losing heat." The drop is real heat transfer: the dissolving
salt **takes** energy from the water to pull its particles apart and into
solution, so the water's temperature falls. The energy has not disappeared —
it has become chemical energy in the solution, exactly the reverse of the
exothermic bookkeeping.
:::

:::safety
Wear eye protection and avoid skin contact with the salts and their
solutions.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.2 + 3.4 + 3.8 dissolving-calorimetry items.
Recalculate with 6.40 g of ammonium chloride in 100 cm³ of water falling
from 19.6 °C to 15.6 °C: show Q, n and the signed ∆H. Check: Q = 1672 J,
n = 0.1196 mol, ∆H ≈ +14.0 kJ/mol. Then state whether potassium chloride
dissolving exothermically would give a maximum or minimum reading.
:::

sections.title: Practical: measuring the enthalpy change of neutralisation
sections.markdown:
The reaction between an alkali and an acid is essentially the reaction
between hydroxide ions and hydrogen ions to form water:

OH⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) → H₂O(l)

For the potassium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid example, suppose you know
the concentration of the potassium hydroxide but are not so sure of the
dilute hydrochloric acid — the label has gone missing. The following method
finds the unknown concentration **and** the heat released, in one run:

1. Place a polystyrene cup in a 250 cm³ glass beaker.
2. Transfer **25 cm³ of 2.00 mol/dm³ potassium hydroxide** into the cup.
3. Record the initial temperature.
4. Fill a burette with **50.00 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid**.
5. Use the burette to add **5.00 cm³** of the acid to the potassium
   hydroxide.
6. Stir vigorously and record the maximum temperature reached.
7. Keep adding further **5.00 cm³ portions**, stirring and recording the
   maximum temperature each time, until 50.00 cm³ in total has been added.

Plot the temperature of the mixture against the volume of acid added. The
shape tells the story: the temperature **increases at first** because the
acid reacts with the alkali and gives out heat; once all the alkali has been
used up, further additions are just cold acid poured into warm solution —
nothing left to react with — so the temperature **goes down**.

Draw **two lines of best fit**, one through the rising points and one
through the falling points: the point where the lines cross represents
**complete [[neutralisation]]**. Reading from the graph, the maximum temperature
is 31.8 °C, reached when 28.00 cm³ of acid has been added (the initial
temperature for the ∆T is 19.3 °C).

:::worked-example
**Calculate the heat released per mole and the unknown acid concentration.**

*Step 1 — heat given out.* Total volume at neutralisation = 25 + 28 = 53 cm³:

Q = mc∆T = 53 × 4.18 × (31.8 − 19.3) = 2769.3 J = **2.7693 kJ**

(Assumptions as always: density of the mixture = 1 g/cm³, and specific heat
capacity = that of water because the neutralised solution is mostly water.)

*Step 2 — moles.* Moles of KOH = (25 ÷ 1000) × 2.00 = **0.0500 mol**. At the
neutralisation point the moles of HCl are **exactly the same** — that is
what the crossing point guarantees.

*Step 3 — the [[molar-enthalpy-change]].* The heat released when 1 mole of
KOH reacts with 1 mole of HCl:

∆H = 2.7693 ÷ 0.0500 = **−55.4 kJ/mol**

KOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → KCl(aq) + H₂O(l)   ∆H = −55.4 kJ/mol

The negative sign shows heat is released in this exothermic neutralisation.

*Step 4 — the unknown concentration.* 28.00 cm³ of acid contained the
0.0500 mol of HCl:

concentration = moles ÷ volume in dm³ = 0.0500 ÷ (28.00 ÷ 1000) = 0.0500 ÷
0.02800 = **1.79 mol/dm³**

One accuracy footnote: strictly, the water formed would first appear as
steam, and extra heat is given out when steam condenses to liquid water —
the attraction forces between molecules form exothermically. At this level
the value is taken for the liquid product.
:::

:::key-point
The two-lines-of-best-fit construction exists to fix the true neutralisation
point: the crossing volume is where moles of acid = moles of alkali, which
is why the HCl moles can be read off the KOH moles without knowing the acid
concentration in advance.
:::

:::exam-hint
This experiment is the richest mark-scheme target in the chapter. Know the
graph shape and its explanation (rises — exothermic neutralisation; falls —
cold acid diluting warm mixture with nothing left to react), the
two-best-fit-lines crossing construction, and the neat two-in-one finish:
∆H = −55.4 kJ/mol **and** the acid concentration 1.79 mol/dm³ from the same
run. When asked why the temperature falls after neutralisation, the phrase
"no further reaction — only dilution with cold acid" is the mark.
:::

:::misconception
"The maximum temperature must be at the largest volume of acid added."
After the crossing point you are adding cold acid to a warm, spent mixture —
each 5.00 cm³ portion drags the temperature down further. The peak sits at
the **neutralisation volume** (28.00 cm³ here), which is smaller than the
50.00 cm³ delivered in total; that is the entire logic of finding the
crossing point.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.2 + 3.4 + 3.8 neutralisation-calorimetry items.
Sketch the temperature-versus-volume graph from memory with both best-fit
lines, calculate n(KOH), and show how the unknown HCl concentration follows
from the crossing volume. Check: n(KOH) = 0.0500 mol; if the crossing came
at 25.00 cm³, the acid would be 2.00 mol/dm³.
:::

sections.title: Why do reactions give out or absorb heat?
sections.markdown:
During chemical reactions, bonds in the reactants have to be broken and new
ones formed to make the products. The whole energy story of every reaction
rests on two facts:

**Breaking bonds needs energy — endothermic.**
**Making bonds releases energy — exothermic.**

Think about hydrogen burning in oxygen to make water:

2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)

Energy has to be supplied to break the bonds in the hydrogen molecules and
in the oxygen molecule. Energy is released when new bonds form between the
hydrogen and oxygen atoms inside the water molecules. In this particular
reaction the products are more stable than the reactants: the total energy
**released** when the covalent bonds form in the water molecules is **more
than** the energy **required** to break the covalent bonds in the hydrogen
and oxygen molecules. Released > absorbed, so the reaction is
[[exothermic]] overall.

Heating calcium carbonate runs the ledger the other way. Breaking up the
original bonds in the compound **uses more energy** than is obtained when
the new ones are made: the reactants are more stable than the products, so
when the reaction finishes more energy has been absorbed than released — an
[[endothermic]] change.

This is also where the small starting push many reactions need comes from:
energy is required to begin breaking the reactant bonds even in a reaction
that releases heat overall (the quantity is called the [[activation-energy]]
and this chapter's bond-energy arithmetic is what lets you account for it).
But the classification of a reaction depends only on the **balance**:
absorbed minus released.

- released **>** absorbed → exothermic, ∆H negative, products more stable.
- absorbed **>** released → endothermic, ∆H positive, products less stable.

:::key-point
The sign of ∆H is decided by competition: energy in to break reactant bonds
versus energy out from making product bonds. Whichever term is bigger wins
the sign — and the winner also decides which side of the energy level
diagram sits higher.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Explain, in terms of breaking and making bonds, why this reaction is
exothermic" has a three-part mark scheme: (1) bond breaking is endothermic /
needs energy, (2) bond making is exothermic / releases energy, (3) more
energy is released making the new bonds than is needed to break the original
ones. All three sentences, in that order. Omitting the comparison sentence
is the most common way to drop the third mark — naming both processes is not
the same as comparing them.
:::

:::misconception
"Bonds are like springs — breaking them must release the stored energy."
Everyday intuition says breaking things releases energy (snapping a stick,
smashing a plate), but chemical bonds work the opposite way: the bond is the
*low-energy arrangement*, so pulling it apart **costs** energy, and forming
it **pays** energy back. That inversion is the single most examined idea in
the chemistry-only half of this chapter.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.6C bond-breaking/making items. Write the two
law-statements (breaking/making) from memory, apply them to explain why
hydrogen burning is exothermic, and why calcium carbonate decomposition is
endothermic — one sentence each with the comparison word *more* or *less*
included.
:::

sections.title: Bond energies
sections.markdown:
Breaking chemical bonds requires energy, and the stronger the bond, the
more energy is needed to break it. The [[bond-energy]] is defined as **the
amount of energy needed to break 1 mole of covalent bonds in gaseous
molecules**, measured in kJ/mol. The same number works in reverse: the bond
energy is also the amount of energy released when 1 mole of those bonds
**forms**.

Two examples anchor the idea. The Cl–Cl bond energy is **243 kJ/mol**: it
takes 243 kJ to break all the Cl–Cl bonds in 1 mole of chlorine gas,
splitting each molecule into two chlorine atoms — and if those atoms
recombine into their original molecules, exactly 243 kJ is released again.
The H–Cl bond energy is **432 kJ/mol**: if you see 2HCl(g) in an equation,
it takes 2 × 432 kJ to break all the H–Cl bonds in the two moles of hydrogen
chloride — or 2 × 432 kJ will be released when 2HCl(g) is formed from H and
Cl atoms. The coefficient in front multiplies the bond energy; that one
sentence is the whole counting rule of the next section.

| Bond | C–H | C–Cl | I–Cl | Cl–Cl | I–I | H–Cl | H–I |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bond energy / kJ/mol | 413 | 346 | 234 | 243 | 151 | 432 | 298 |

Some bonds are much stronger than others. A striking comparison from the
table: the bond between iodine and hydrogen (298 kJ/mol) is about **twice as
strong** as the bond between two iodine atoms (151 kJ/mol).

Bond energies can be used to calculate how much heat will be absorbed or
released during reactions of **covalent molecules**. If a reaction involves
ionic compounds, different energy terms are needed — beyond International
GCSE. The method is an estimate by dismantling and rebuilding: calculate how
much energy would be needed to break the reactants up into individual atoms,
then how much would be given out when those atoms recombine into the new
arrangements of the products.

:::exam-hint
Bond-energy questions always supply the table — you never memorise values.
What you must bring is the counting discipline: multiply each bond energy by
**how many moles of that bond** appear in the balanced equation. The 1-mole
definition is also a mark: writing "energy to break a bond" instead of
"energy to break **1 mole** of bonds in gaseous molecules" loses the
definition mark. Note the word *gaseous* — it constrains where the method is
valid (see the next section's worked example).
:::

:::misconception
"A bond energy of 432 kJ/mol for H–Cl means one HCl molecule needs 432 kJ
to break." The value is per **mole** of bonds — one molecule needs 432 kJ
divided by the Avogadro number, an utterly tiny amount. All bond-energy
arithmetic runs in per-mole quantities multiplied by the
equation's coefficients.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.7C bond-energy-definition items. State the
definition of bond energy with its unit, interpret Cl–Cl = 243 kJ/mol in
both directions (breaking and forming), and calculate the energy to break
all the bonds in 2 moles of HCl gas.
:::

sections.title: Bond-energy calculations
sections.markdown:
The calculation recipe has one sign rule and two sums. When energy is given
out you show it with a **negative** sign; when energy is taken in, positive.
Then:

- **energy needed to break all the bonds in the reactants** — every term
  positive;
- **energy released when the new bonds are made in the products** — every
  term negative;
- **overall change = (energy in to break) + (energy out to make)** — a
  positive total means the reaction is endothermic, a negative total
  exothermic.

A quick illustration of the rule: if breaking all the reactant bonds costs
+1000 kJ and making the product bonds releases −1200 kJ, the overall change
is +1000 + (−1200) = **−200 kJ** — the reaction releases 200 kJ of energy
overall, so it is exothermic.

:::worked-example
**Methane reacts with chlorine in the presence of ultraviolet light to
produce chloromethane and hydrogen chloride.** You can imagine all the bonds
being broken in the methane and chlorine, and then being reformed in new
ways in the products. Calculate the overall energy change.

Bonds that need to be broken (endothermic):

| Bond | Count | Sum |
|---|---|---|
| 4 C–H | 4 × (+413) | +1652 kJ |
| 1 Cl–Cl | 1 × (+243) | +243 kJ |
| | **total in** | **+1895 kJ** |

New bonds made (exothermic):

| Bond | Count | Sum |
|---|---|---|
| 3 C–H | 3 × (−413) | −1239 kJ |
| 1 C–Cl | 1 × (−346) | −346 kJ |
| 1 H–Cl | 1 × (−432) | −432 kJ |
| | **total out** | **−2017 kJ** |

More energy is released when bonds are formed than is required to break
them, so the reaction releases energy overall: it is exothermic.

Overall energy change = +1895 + (−2017) = **−122 kJ**

The negative sign of the answer shows that, overall, heat is given out as
the bonds rearrange.
:::

Two honesty notes belong beside every bond-energy answer. First, [[bond-energy]]
calculations only ever give **estimates**: the strength of a bond varies
slightly depending on what else is around it in the molecule, so quoted bond
energies are **average** values — good, but not perfect. Enthalpy changes
measured by the calorimetry experiments of this chapter are more specific for
particular compounds. Second, the "break everything, rebuild everything"
route is an **imaginary** one — the real reaction does not actually happen
by all the bonds being broken this way. That does not matter: the overall
amount of heat released or absorbed is the same however you do the reaction,
as long as the reactants and products are the same. That fact is
[[hesss-law]], which you will meet again if you take chemistry further.

:::worked-example
**Combustion of methane.** The equation is:

CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g)

| Bond | C–H | O=O | C=O | O–H |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bond energy / kJ/mol | 413 | 498 | 743 | 464 |

Start by drawing out the structures showing all the bonds, so the bond
counts are right: CH₄ holds 4 C–H; the two O₂ molecules hold 2 O=O
double bonds (498 kJ/mol is the energy to break the **whole** double bond);
CO₂ holds 2 C=O; the two H₂O molecules hold 4 O–H.

Bonds that need to be broken (endothermic):

4 C–H = 4 × (+413) = +1652 kJ
2 O=O = 2 × (+498) = +996 kJ
**total in = +2648 kJ**

New bonds made (exothermic):

2 C=O = 2 × (−743) = −1486 kJ
4 O–H = 4 × (−464) = −1856 kJ
**total out = −3342 kJ**

Enthalpy change = +2648 + (−3342) = **−694 kJ/mol**

More energy is released when bonds are formed than is required to break
them: the reaction is exothermic. Energy is given out as the reactants are
converted to the products, so the products must have less energy than the
reactants — the products are more stable, and an energy level diagram for
this reaction shows the products level sitting below the reactants level,
with a downward arrow and ∆H = −694 kJ/mol.

The reaction is written with H₂O(g) rather than H₂O(l) deliberately: bond
energies can only be used for **gaseous** molecules. Finding the enthalpy
change for the same reaction forming liquid water would need the energy
released by H₂O(g) → H₂O(l) as well — beyond International GCSE.
:::

:::exam-hint
Paper 2C marks these in four slots: correct bond **counts** from the drawn-out
structures (the balancing coefficients multiply the bonds — 2O₂ means 2
O=O, and 2H₂O means 4 O–H), correct signs (+ in, − out), the addition to a
total, and the exothermic/endothermic verdict tied to the sign. Draw the
molecules first: every miscounted bond in this question family traces back
to skipping the structures. If an energy level diagram is required, the
sign of your total dictates which level the products occupy.
:::

:::misconception
"O=O at 498 kJ/mol breaks into two O– bonds worth 249 kJ each, so count the
double bond as two single bonds." The 498 kJ/mol is the energy to break the
**whole double bond at once** — count one O=O per oxygen molecule. Bond
tables list whole bonds (single or double as printed); inventing half-values
or counting double bonds twice is the standard arithmetic corruption in this
question.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.7C bond-energy-calculation items. Recalculate the
methane + chlorine example with the C–H value 410 kJ/mol: your totals are
+1883 in and −2008 out, giving −125 kJ — confirm the sign does not change.
Then state the two honesty notes (average values; imaginary route) in one
sentence each.
:::

sections.title: Looking ahead: entropy
sections.markdown:
Many reactions you meet at International GCSE are exothermic — combustion
and neutralisation, for instance. Despite needing a small amount of energy
to get started (the [[activation-energy]]), these reactions release heat
energy overall because the products are more stable than the reactants.
Enthalpy is clearly a driving force: reactions that give out heat happen
readily.

But endothermic processes happen too. Dissolving ammonium nitrate in water
lowers the temperature of the solution — yet it dissolves anyway, pulling
heat out of its surroundings and still going. How? A second factor is at
work: [[entropy]].

Entropy is a measure of **the number of ways of distributing the energy in
a system**. It is greater in a more disordered system, because the energy
can be dispersed more flexibly. The ordering runs solid → liquid → gas:
solids have lower entropy than liquids, and liquids lower entropy than
gases — a gas's particles roam freely, so its energy has the most ways to
be shared out.

If the entropy of a system **increases** during a change, the change is more
likely to happen. When ammonium nitrate dissolves, although the process is
endothermic, the NH₄⁺ and NO₃⁻ ions in the giant ionic lattice become
separated from each other and gain freedom of movement in the water — the
entropy of the system increases enough to outweigh the enthalpy
unfavourability. The same logic explains a kitchen classic: the reaction
between baking soda and vinegar (an endothermic reaction that proceeds
spontaneously, fizzing out carbon dioxide gas) — producing a gas increases
the entropy of the system, and the increase carries the change.

You do not need to calculate entropy at this level. What the examiners want
is the concept: enthalpy is not the only driving force, and an increase in
disorder can power changes that absorb heat.

:::exam-hint
This is enrichment, not a numbered specification point — but it earns
extension credit and it future-proofs the explanation questions. If asked
"why does ammonium nitrate dissolve even though the process is endothermic?",
the mature two-part answer is: the dissolving is endothermic, but the ions
leaving the lattice for the solution increases the entropy of the system,
and that increase outweighs the enthalpy change. The same pattern answers
for any spontaneous endothermic change that produces a gas.
:::

:::misconception
"Endothermic changes cannot happen by themselves because they need heat
pumped in." They cannot happen if enthalpy were the only driving force —
but disorder counts too. A change that absorbs heat can still run on its
own when it increases the number of ways the system's energy can be
distributed: ammonium nitrate dissolving in cool water is the standard
proof.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: extension entropy items. Define entropy in one sentence,
order the three states of matter by entropy, and explain in two sentences
why ammonium nitrate dissolves in water even though the temperature drops.
:::

sections.title: Chapter 19 questions
sections.markdown:
You have the complete toolkit now: the exothermic/endothermic split, the
∆H sign convention, the Q = mc∆T and ∆H = Q ÷ n pair, four calorimetry
setups with their assumptions and errors, and — for Paper 2C — energy level
diagrams and bond-energy arithmetic. The question bank for this chapter
joins the platform by the specification points below, so every practice
item you are served targets exactly the skills these sections taught.

Before you open the question bank, audit yourself against the chapter's
core moves. Can you define both reaction types with the heat-flow direction?
Can you run a five-step combustion calculation from a burner data table?
Can you state the two solution-calorimetry assumptions and the two errors
that make combustion results less exothermic? On the Paper 2C track: can
you draw both energy level diagrams with every label, and run a bond-energy
sum with correct counts and signs? Anything that wobbled is a section to
revisit, not a reason to start over.

:::summary
- **[[exothermic]]**: heat given out to the surroundings, temperature rises,
  products have less chemical energy (more stable), ∆H negative. Families:
  combustion, metal + acid, neutralisation, displacement.
- **[[endothermic]]**: heat taken in from the surroundings, temperature
  falls, products have more chemical energy (less stable), ∆H positive.
  Example: thermal decomposition of carbonates — heating must continue
  throughout. Not everything that needs a flame to start is endothermic.
- **[[enthalpy-change]] ∆H**: heat taken in or given out per the equation's
  amounts, read from the reactants' point of view, units kJ/mol; you can
  only measure the change, never the absolute enthalpy.
- **Q = mc∆T** converts a temperature change of a known mass (usually
  water, c = 4.18 J/g/°C) into heat energy; ∆H = Q ÷ n converts it to a
  per-mole value with the sign from the temperature trend.
- **Calorimetry families**: combustion (spirit burner + copper can; lid,
  shielding, stir), displacement (polystyrene cup; excess metal; divide by
  the limiting reactant), dissolving (physical process; minimum
  temperature; read the sign carefully), neutralisation (two best-fit
  lines; crossing point = complete neutralisation; doubles as an unknown
  concentration method).
- **Evaluation**: combustion values come out less exothermic than data
  books because of heat loss and incomplete combustion (yellow-orange
  flame, soot); longer alcohol chains burn more exothermically, rising
  regularly with each extra CH₂.
- **Paper 2C**: energy level diagrams (label both axes; products' level
  follows the sign of ∆H); bond-breaking endothermic, bond-making
  exothermic; bond energies are per-mole averages for gaseous molecules —
  count bonds from drawn-out structures, add +in and −out, and the total's
  sign classifies the reaction.
:::

:::can-you
- Define exothermic and endothermic reactions and give two balanced
  equations for each?
- Draw and label energy level diagrams for both types (Paper 2C)?
- Calculate Q from mc∆T and quote it with the right sign and units?
- Convert Q into a molar enthalpy change, dividing by the **limiting**
  reactant's moles?
- Describe all four calorimetry procedures with their key controls and
  assumptions?
- Explain why a combustion experiment under-reads, with evidence?
- Calculate an overall enthalpy change from bond energies, including
  double bonds and balancing coefficients (Paper 2C)?
:::

:::exam-hint
Past-paper items for this chapter cluster into three question shapes: a
calculate-from-data Q = mc∆T / ∆H = Q ÷ n chain (always with a sign mark),
a describe-the-method-and-its-errors practical question (assumptions,
improvements, evidence of incomplete combustion), and the Paper 2C
diagram-plus-bond-energy pair. Practise all three shapes against the
clock — and remember the chapter-wide discipline: sign first, then size.
:::

:::misconception
"Revising the formulas is enough for this chapter." The formula questions
are the predictable half. The unpredictable half is the practical
understanding — which mass goes into m, why the lid stays on the burner,
why two lines of best fit, why the zinc is in excess. The examiner tests
the *why* behind every step; the sections in this chapter were written so
each step's reason is one sentence you can quote.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.1–3.8 chapter assessment items. Work through the
can-you list honestly, marking each item secure or shaky, then take the
platform's spec-joined question set for 3.2–3.4 first (the calculation
chain earns the most marks per minute of revision).
:::
